paragraphs.text: Commemoration and life of our blessed teacher Constantine the Philosopher, the first teacher of the Slavic people. Give your blessing.

God, merciful and compassionate, waits for human repentance, so that all might be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, for he does not desire the sinner's death, but his repentance and life, even if he adds evil upon evil. He does not abandon the human race to fall away through weakness, fall into the devil's snare, and perish, but in every age and season he never ceases to show us abundant grace, as from the beginning down to the present, choosing out of this tumultuous life first patriarchs and fathers, and after them prophets, and after these apostles and martyrs, righteous men and teachers.
For the Lord knows his own, those who belong to him, as he said: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them and call them by name, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life."

This he also did in our generation, raising up for us such a teacher, who enlightened our people, for we had darkened our minds through weakness, or rather through the devil's deceit, and had not wished to walk in the light of God's commandments.

His life, briefly recounted as it happened, makes this clear, so that anyone who wishes may hear it and imitate him, embracing diligence and casting off laziness, as the apostle said: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ."
In the city of Thessalonica there was a certain man of noble birth and wealth named Leo. He held the rank of drungarius under the military governor.

He was devout, keeping all God's commandments fully, like Job of old. Living with his wife, he fathered seven children, of whom the youngest, the seventh, was Constantine the Philosopher, our guide and teacher.
When his mother gave birth to him, she handed him to a wet nurse to nurse him; but the child would not take any other woman's breast, only his mother's, until he was weaned.
This happened through God's providence, so that a good shoot might come from a good root.

After this, those good parents agreed not to have marital relations, keeping themselves chaste, and thus they lived in the Lord for fourteen years, until death parted them, never breaking that agreement.
When he was about to go to judgment, this child's mother wept, saying: "I am not worried about anything except this one little child, and how he will be cared for."
He said: "Believe me, wife, I trust in God that he will give him as his father and guardian the one who also cares for all Christians."
And this indeed came to pass.
When the boy was seven years old, he had a dream and told his father and mother, saying:
"The military governor gathered all the maidens of our city and said to me: 'Choose from among them whichever you wish as your companion and as a helper suited to you.'"

After looking over and examining them all, I saw one who was more beautiful than all the others, with a radiant face, richly adorned with gold necklaces, pearls, and every kind of beauty. Her name was Sophia, which means Wisdom. I chose her.
When his parents heard these words, they said to him:
My son, keep your father's law, and do not reject your mother's instruction.
For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is a light.
Say to wisdom, “Be my sister,” and make wisdom your close companion.
For wisdom shines more brightly than the sun; and if you take her to yourself as a wife, you will be delivered through her from much evil.
When they sent him to be taught, he surpassed all the other pupils in his studies, learning so quickly by heart that it was a marvel.

One day, as it is customary for rich men's sons to amuse themselves by hunting, he went out into the countryside with them, taking his sparrowhawk. When he released it, a wind arose by God's providence, caught it up, and carried it away.
Because of this, the boy fell into despondency and sorrow and did not eat for two days.
For in his love for mankind, the merciful God did not allow him to become attached to worldly things, but easily caught him.
Just as in ancient times he caught Placidus through a deer while he was hunting, so he caught this boy through a sparrowhawk.
Reflecting within himself on the vanity of this life, he lamented, saying:
Is this what life is like, that sorrow comes in place of joy?
From this day on I will take another path, one better than this, and I will not spend my days amid the turmoil of this life.
Reflecting on these things, he sat in his house, learning by heart the books of Saint Gregory the Theologian. He made the sign of the cross on the wall and wrote this praise of Saint Gregory:
O Gregory, a man in body but an angel in soul!
Though you were a man in body, you proved to be an angel, for your lips glorify God like one of the seraphim and enlighten the whole world with the teaching of the true faith.
Therefore receive me too, as I fall before you with love and faith, and be my teacher and enlightener. Such were the words he addressed to him.
As he delved into many discourses and lofty thought [?], he could not understand their depths and fell into great despondency.
There was a foreigner there who knew grammar. He went to him and begged him, falling at his feet and placing himself in his care:
Teach me the art of grammar thoroughly.
But the man, having buried his talent, said to him: Young man, do not trouble yourself. I have firmly resolved never to teach this to anyone as long as I live.
Again the boy bowed before him and said with tears: Take my entire share of my father's estate, everything that is due to me, but teach me.
But he did not wish to listen to him, and went to his own home, where he continued in prayer, so that he might obtain his heart’s desire.
And God soon fulfilled the desire of those who fear him.
For the emperor’s administrator, who is called the logothete, heard about his beauty, wisdom, and devotion to learning, which were united in him, and sent for him to study alongside the emperor.
When the boy heard this, he joyfully set out on his journey. Along the way he bowed down and offered a prayer, saying:

“God of our fathers and Lord of mercy, who made all things by your word and fashioned humanity by your wisdom, so that humanity might rule over the creatures you made, give me the wisdom that is beside your thrones, so that I may understand what is pleasing to you and be saved.
For I am your servant and the son of your maidservant.”
After reciting the rest of Solomon’s prayer as well, he rose and said, “Amen.”
When he arrived in Constantinople, they entrusted him to teachers to be educated. In three months he mastered grammar and began the other subjects.

He studied Homer and geometry, and under Leo and Photius he studied dialectic [?] and all the philosophical disciplines, and in addition to these, rhetoric, arithmetic, astronomy, music, and all the other Greek arts.
He mastered them all as though he were learning only one of them.
For quickness was joined with diligence, each striving to outdo the other, and through these learning and the arts are brought to perfection.

But even more than his learning, he displayed a gentle manner, associating with those whose company was more beneficial, and avoiding those who turned toward crooked ways, seeking to exchange earthly things for heavenly things, to fly free of this body and live with God.
Seeing what he was like, the logothete gave him authority over his household and permission to enter the emperor’s palace freely.
Once he questioned him, saying, “Philosopher, I would like to know what philosophy is.”

With his quick mind, he immediately replied, “Knowledge of divine and human things, through which a person can draw as near to God as possible, for it teaches a person through deeds to be in the image and likeness of the one who created him.”
This made that great and honored man love him even more, and he questioned him further about it.
He then gave him instruction in philosophy, explaining profound meaning in a few words.
As he continued to live in purity, greatly pleasing God, he became all the more beloved by everyone.
The logothete treated him with every mark of reverent honor and offered him much gold, but he would not accept it.

Once he said to him, “Your beauty and wisdom compel me to love you beyond measure. Now I have a spiritual daughter whom I received from the baptismal font, beautiful and wealthy, and from a good and distinguished family. If you wish, I will give her to you as your wife.” Now accept great honor and a governorship from the emperor, and expect still greater things, for you will soon become a general.

The philosopher answered him: “The gift is indeed great for those who need it, but for me nothing is greater than learning. By gaining understanding through it, I wish to seek the honor and wealth of my forefathers.”

When the logothete heard his answer, he went to the empress and said: “This young philosopher has no love for this life. Let us therefore not allow him to withdraw from society, but have him tonsured and ordained a priest and assign him a post, so that he may be the patriarch’s librarian at Hagia Sophia. Perhaps we can at least keep him this way.”
And this is what they did with him.
But after remaining with him in this position for a short time, he went to the narrow sea and hid in a monastery.
They searched for him for six months and only with difficulty found him.
Unable to compel him to return to that post, they begged him to accept a teaching chair and teach philosophy to natives and foreigners, with every assistance and support.
He agreed to this.
Now the patriarch Annius had stirred up a heresy, saying: “Do not honor the holy icons.”
They assembled a council, exposed the error of his teaching, and drove him from his throne.
But he said: “They drove me out by force, not by refuting me, for no one can oppose my arguments.”
The emperor and the patricians arranged for the philosopher to confront him and sent him with this message: “If you can refute this young man, you will receive your throne back.”
When he saw that the philosopher was young in body, he said to him and those sent with him: “None of you is worthy even to be my footstool. How, then, could I be willing to debate with you?”
The philosopher said to him: “Do not cling to human custom, but look to God’s commandments.
For just as you were formed by God from earth and a soul, so were we all.
So look at the earth, man, and do not be proud.”
Annius answered again: “It is not fitting to seek flowers in autumn, nor to drive an old man into battle as though he were some young Nestor.”
The philosopher answered him: “You yourself are finding grounds for your own condemnation.
Tell me, at what age is the soul stronger than the body?”
He said: “In old age.”
The philosopher said: “Then into what sort of battle are we driving you, a bodily one or a spiritual one?”
He said: “A spiritual one.”
The philosopher answered, “So now you want to be the stronger one.”
“Do not tell us such parables, for we are not looking for flowers out of season, nor are we driving you into battle.”

The old man was ashamed and turned the conversation to another subject, saying, “Tell me, young man: when a cross is broken, we neither bow down to it nor kiss it. But you are not ashamed to honor an icon even if it is painted only down to the chest?”

The philosopher answered, “A cross has four parts, and if one of its parts is missing, it no longer displays its own form. But an icon displays the likeness of the person depicted through the face alone. Whoever looks at it sees neither a lion’s face nor a lynx’s, but the likeness of the original.”
Again the old man said, “Why do we bow down to a cross without an inscription, even though there have been other crosses as well?
Yet if an icon does not bear the written name of the person whose likeness it is, you do not honor it?”
The philosopher answered, “Every cross has a form like that of Christ’s cross, but not all icons have the same form.”
The old man said, “Since God said to Moses, ‘You shall not make every kind of likeness,’ how can you make them and bow down to them?”
The philosopher answered him, “If he had said, ‘You shall not make any likeness whatsoever,’ your objection would be right. But he said, ‘Not every kind,’ meaning an unworthy one.”
Unable to argue against this, the old man fell silent and was put to shame.
After this, the Hagarenes, called Saracens, raised a blasphemous objection to the oneness of God in the Holy Trinity, saying:
“How is it that you Christians, while believing in one God, divide him again into three, saying that he is Father, Son, and Spirit?
If you can explain this clearly, send men who can speak about it and refute us.”
The philosopher was then twenty-four years old.
The emperor convened a council, summoned him, and said to him, “Do you hear, philosopher, what the impure Hagarenes are saying against our faith?

Since you are a servant and disciple of the Holy Trinity, go and oppose them. And may God, who brings everything to completion, who is glorified in the Trinity as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, grant you grace and power in your words, so that he may reveal you as another, new David against Goliath, victorious with three stones, and bring you back to us, making you worthy also of the kingdom of heaven.”
Hearing this, he answered, “I gladly go for the Christian faith.
For what is sweeter to me in this world than to live and die for the Holy Trinity?”
They assigned an imperial secretary and George to accompany him. [?]
When they arrived there, images of demons had been painted on the outside of all the Christians’ doors, making a spectacle of them and mocking them.
They questioned the philosopher, saying, “Can you understand, philosopher, what this sign means?”
He said, “I see an image of a demon, and I think that Christians live inside there. The demons, unable to live with them, flee outside, away from them.
But wherever this sign is absent, they are inside there with them.”
At dinner, the Hagarenes sitting there—clever people, learned in books, geometry, astronomy, and other branches of knowledge—tested him and questioned him, saying:
“Do you see, philosopher, this marvelous wonder: how the prophet Muhammad brought us good news from God and converted many peoples? We all observe the law without transgressing anything.
But you who follow Christ’s law observe it and act in different ways, one this way and another that way, as each of you pleases.”
The philosopher answered them, “Our God is like the depths of the sea, and the prophet says of him:
‘Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken from the earth.’

Many enter those depths in search of him, and those strong in understanding, receiving spiritual riches with his help, swim across and return. But the weak attempt to cross as though in rotten ships: some drown, while others barely catch their breath after great effort, tossed about in their feeble laziness.
Your teaching, however, is plain and easy, something anyone, small or great, can leap across.
For it does not go beyond ordinary human behavior, but only requires what a person can do; he has commanded you nothing.
Since he has not restrained anger and lust, but has allowed them, into what abyss will he cast you [?]?
Let anyone with understanding consider this.
Christ, however, does not act this way, but raises what is heavy from below to the heights through faith and godly deeds.

For, being the Creator of all, he created the human being between angels and beasts, distinguishing him from beasts by speech and understanding, and from angels by anger and lust. Whichever rank someone approaches, he shares more in it, whether the higher or the lower.”
They questioned him again: “Since God is one, how do you glorify him as three? Tell us, if you know.
For you name the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.
If you speak this way, then give him a wife too, so that many gods may be bred from this.”
The philosopher answered them, “Do not utter such shameful blasphemies.
We have been well taught by the prophets, the fathers, and the teachers to glorify the Trinity: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, three persons in one being.

That Word took flesh in a virgin and was born for our salvation, as Muhammad, your prophet, also bears witness, writing as follows: ‘We sent our Spirit to the virgin, willing that she should give birth.’
From this I will give you an explanation of the Trinity.”
Struck by these words, they turned to other matters, saying, “If it is as you say, guest, and Christ is your God, why do you not do as he commands?”
“For it is written in the books of the Gospel that you should pray for your enemies, do good to those who hate and persecute you, and turn your cheek to those who strike you.”
“But you do not act this way; instead, you sharpen weapons against those who do such things to you.”
The philosopher answered them, “When there are two commandments in the law, who shows himself to fulfill the law: someone who keeps one, or someone who keeps both?”
They answered, “Someone who keeps both.”
The philosopher said, “God has said, ‘Pray for those who mistreat you.’” “He has also said, ‘No one can show greater love in this life than to lay down his life for his friends.’”
“We do this for our friends, so that their souls may not be taken captive along with their bodies.”
Again they said, “Christ paid tribute for himself and for others. Why do you not do the same?”
“And even if you defend yourselves, why do you not at least pay tribute to so great and powerful an Ishmaelite nation on behalf of your brothers and friends?”
“We ask little—only one gold coin—and, as long as the whole earth stands, we will keep peace between us as no one else does.”
The philosopher answered, “If someone following a teacher wishes to walk in the same footsteps as his teacher, and another meets him and turns him aside, is that person his friend or his enemy?”
They answered, “An enemy?”
The philosopher said, “When Christ paid tribute, which kingdom was it: the Ishmaelite or the Roman?”
They answered, “The Roman.”
He said, “Therefore you should not reproach us, since we all pay tribute to the Romans.”
After this they asked many other questions, testing him in all the arts that they themselves knew.
He explained everything to them, overcoming them in these matters as well.
They said to him, “How do you know all these things?”
The philosopher said, “A certain man drew water from the sea and carried it in a little bag. He boasted, saying to travelers, ‘Do you see this water, which no one has except me?’”
“Then a man from the seacoast came and said to him, ‘Are you acting like a madman, boasting only of a stinking little bag, when we have an ocean of this?’”
“You act in the same way, yet all the arts have come from us.”

After this, performing wonders, they showed him a planted garden springing up from the ground at times. When he explained to them how this happened, they then showed him all their wealth and buildings adorned with gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls, saying:
“Look, philosopher, at this marvelous wonder, the great power and abundant wealth of the Commander of the Faithful, the ruler of the Saracens.”
He said to them, “This is nothing remarkable. Glory and praise belong to God, who made all these things and gave them for people’s comfort; for they belong to him and to no one else.”
Later, reverting to their wickedness, they gave him poison to drink.
But the merciful God, who said, “Even if you drink something deadly, it will not harm you,” delivered him too and brought him back safely to his own country.

And again, not long afterward, he renounced everything belonging to this life and settled in one place in quiet, attending only to himself and keeping nothing for the next day, but giving everything away to the poor and casting his cares upon God, who cares for everyone each day.

Once, on a holy day, his servant complained to him, “We have nothing for such an honored day.” He said to him, “He who once fed the Israelites in the wilderness will also give us food here. But go and invite at least five poor men, trusting in God’s help.”
When the time for the midday meal came, a man immediately brought [?] a load of all kinds of food and ten gold coins.
And he gave praise to God for all these things.
He went to Olympus, to his brother Methodius, and began to live there, praying to God without ceasing and conversing only with books.
Envoys came to the emperor from the Khazars, saying, “From the beginning we have known one God, who is above all, and we worship him facing east, though we also observe other shameful customs.

The Jews are urging us to accept their faith and practices, while the Saracens, on the other side, offer peace and many gifts and try to draw us to their faith, saying, ‘Our faith is better than that of all other nations.’
For this reason we send to you, maintaining our longstanding friendship and love.
For you are a great nation and hold imperial power from God.
Seeking your counsel, we ask you to send us a learned man. If he refutes the Jews and the Saracens, we will adopt your faith.”
Then the emperor sought out the Philosopher, and when he found him, he told him what the Khazars had said, saying,
“Go, Philosopher, to these people, and with the help of the Holy Trinity, speak and give an answer concerning it; for no one else can do this worthily.”
He said, “If you command it, lord, I will gladly go on such a mission on foot and barefoot, without any of the things that the Lord told his disciples not to carry.”
The emperor answered, “If that is what you wish to do in this matter, you speak well. But bear in mind the power and honor of the empire, and go with honor and imperial support.”
He immediately set out on his journey. When he reached Cherson, he learned the Hebrew language and its writings there, translated the eight parts of the grammar, and gained understanding from it.
A certain Samaritan lived there. He came to him and debated with him, and brought Samaritan books and showed them to him.
The Philosopher asked him for them, shut himself in a room, and devoted himself to prayer. Receiving understanding from God, he began to read the books without error.
When the Samaritan saw this, he cried out in a loud voice and said, “Truly, those who believe in Christ soon receive the Holy Spirit and grace.”
His son was baptized at once, and he himself was baptized after him.

There he found a Gospel book and a Psalter written in Russian letters. He also found a man who spoke that language, and, after speaking with him and grasping the meaning of his speech, he compared it with his own language, distinguishing the letters, vowels and consonants. Keeping up his prayer to God, he soon began to read and interpret, and many marveled at him and praised God.
On hearing that Saint Clement still lay in the sea, he prayed and said: “I believe in God and place my hope in Saint Clement that I shall find him and bring him out of the sea.”

He persuaded the archbishop, together with all the clergy and devout men, and they boarded ships and went to the place, the sea having become very calm. When they arrived, they began to dig, singing as they did so.

At once there was much chrism, like abundant incense, and after this the holy relics appeared. They took them up with great honor and brought them into the city amid the praises of all the citizens, as is written in the account of their discovery.
Now a Khazar commander came with his troops, surrounded a Christian city, and laid siege to it.
When the Philosopher learned of this, he went to him without delay. He spoke with him, offered him words of instruction, and calmed him.
And the commander promised him that he would be baptized.
Then the Philosopher returned to his journey.
While he was praying at the first hour, Hungarians attacked him, howling like wolves and wanting to kill him.
But he was not frightened, nor did he abandon his prayer, calling out only, “Lord, have mercy,” for he had already finished the service.
When they saw him, they grew calm at God’s command and began to bow before him. After hearing words of instruction from his mouth, they let him go with his whole company.
Then he boarded a ship and set out on his journey to the Khazars, toward Lake Maeotis and the Caspian Gates of the Caucasus Mountains.
The Khazars sent a cunning man [?] to meet him. He entered into conversation with him and said:
“Why do you have the bad custom of putting one emperor in another’s place from a different family? We, however, do this according to lineage.”
The Philosopher said to him, “God chose David, who pleased him, and his family in place of Saul, who did nothing pleasing to him.”

The man spoke again: “You hold books in your hands and speak all your parables from them; but we do not do so. We bring forth all wisdom from our breasts, as though we had swallowed it, without priding ourselves on writings as you do.”
The Philosopher said to him, “Here is my answer to you: If you meet a naked man who says, ‘I have many clothes and much gold,’ will you believe him when you see him naked?”
And he said, “No.”
He said to him: “Then I too say to you: if you have swallowed all wisdom, tell us how many generations there were down to Moses and how many years each generation lasted.”
Unable to answer this, he fell silent.
When he arrived there, as they were about to sit down to dinner with the khagan, they asked him: “What is your rank, so that we may seat you in your proper place?”

He said: “I had a grandfather who was very great and glorious, who stood close to the emperor. He willingly rejected the glory given to him and was banished. He went to a foreign land, became poor, and there fathered me.
I seek my grandfather’s former honor and have not managed to obtain any other, for I am Adam’s grandson.”
They answered: “You speak rightly and justly, guest.”
From then on they began to show him honor.
The khagan took a cup and said: “Let us drink in the name of the one God, who made all creation.”

The philosopher took a cup and said: “I drink in the name of the one God and his Word, who made all creation by his Word, by whom the heavens were established, and of the life-giving Spirit, by whom all their host is sustained.”
The khagan answered him: “We say the same things, differing only in this: you glorify the Trinity, while we glorify the one God, having received the Scriptures.”
The philosopher said: “The Scriptures proclaim the Word and the Spirit.
If someone honors you but does not honor your word and the breath of your mouth, while another honors all three, which of the two shows greater honor?”
He said: “The one who honors all three.”
The philosopher answered: “Thus we give greater honor, explaining through facts and listening to the prophets.
For Isaiah said: ‘Listen to me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call: I am the first, and I am forever; now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.’”
The Jews standing around him said to him: “Tell us, then, how can a woman contain in her womb God, whom she cannot even look upon, much less give birth to him?”

The philosopher pointed his finger at the khagan and his chief adviser and said: “If someone says that the chief adviser cannot entertain the khagan, but then says that his lowliest servant can both entertain the khagan and show him honor, what should I call him? Tell me: foolish or sensible?”
They said: “Very foolish indeed.”
The philosopher said to them: “What is the most honorable of all visible creatures?”
They answered him: “The human being, for he was created in God’s image.”

The philosopher said to them again: “Then how are those who say that God cannot be contained in a human being not out of their minds? Yet he contained himself in a bush and in a cloud, appearing to Moses and Job in a whirlwind and smoke.
How can you heal someone else who is sick?”
When the human race had fallen into corruption, from whom could it receive renewal except from the Creator himself?
Answer me: if a physician wishes to apply a plaster to the sick, will he apply it to wood or stone or [?]?
And will he show that the person has been healed by this?

And how did Moses, through the Holy Spirit, say in his prayer, stretching out his hands: “Do not reveal yourself to us any longer in the thunder of stones and the sound of a trumpet, merciful Lord, but dwell within us, taking away our sins.”
For Aquila says this.
And so they departed from the meal, appointing a day on which they would discuss all these things.
When they sat down again with the khagan, the philosopher said: “I am one man among you, without family or friends, and we are debating about God, in whose hands are all things, including our hearts.
As we discuss, let those among you who are skilled in argument say, concerning what they understand, ‘That is so’; and concerning what they do not understand, let them ask for an explanation.”
The Jews answered and said: “We too hold to both the Word and the Spirit in the Scriptures.
Tell us, then, which law did God give to humankind first: that of Moses, or the one you observe?”
The philosopher said: “Are you asking this because you wish to observe the first law?”
They answered: “Yes, for it is right to observe the first.”
The philosopher said: “If you wish to observe the first law, then you must give up circumcision.”
They said: “Why do you say this?”
The philosopher said: “Tell me, concealing nothing: was the first law given in circumcision or in uncircumcision?”
They answered: “We think it was in circumcision.”
The philosopher said: “Did God not first give a law to Noah after the commandment given to Adam and Adam’s fall, calling the law a covenant?
For he said to him: ‘Behold, I will establish my law with you and your descendants and all the earth, maintained through three commandments.’
And: ‘Eat everything, just as you eat green plants: whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, and whatever is in the waters. But do not eat flesh with its blood, which is its life.’
And: ‘Whoever sheds a person’s blood, let his own blood be shed in its place.’
What do you say, in light of this, about observing the first law?”

The Jews answered him: “We observe the first law, that of Moses. God did not call this other one a law, but a covenant, just as the earlier commandment to the man in paradise, and the different one to Abraham—circumcision—were not a law; For the law is one thing and a covenant another. They are different, for the Creator gave each its name.

The philosopher answered them: “I will explain it this way: the law is called a covenant, for God said to Abraham: ‘I give my law in your flesh,’ which he also called a sign, saying that it would be between him and Abraham.

The same God again cries out to Jeremiah: ‘Listen to this covenant, and speak,’ he said, ‘to the men of Judah and those living in Jerusalem, and say to them: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Cursed is the person who does not obey the words of this covenant, which I commanded your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.’”

The Jews answered him: “We too maintain that the law is called a covenant, and all those who followed the law of Moses pleased God. We follow it and expect the same to be true of us, but you have established another law and trample on God’s law.”

The philosopher said to them: “We are right to do so. For if Abraham had not adopted circumcision, but had held to Noah’s covenant, he would not have been called God’s friend. Moses too, who later wrote down the law, did not keep the earlier one.
We likewise follow their example, and having received a law from God, we keep it, so that God’s commandment may remain firmly established.
For when he gave Noah a law, he did not tell him, ‘I will give another also,’ but gave it as one enduring forever for a living soul.
Nor, when he gave promises to Abraham, did he announce to him, ‘I will give another also to Moses.’
Is this how you keep the law?
Yet God cries out through Ezekiel: ‘I will set it aside and give you another.’

And Jeremiah said plainly: ‘Look, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Judah and the house of Israel, not like the covenant I made with your fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not remain in my covenant, and I hated them.

For this is my covenant, which I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law into their minds and write it on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.’

And again the same Jeremiah says: ‘Thus says the Lord: Stand at the roads and look, and ask about the Lord’s eternal paths, and see which is the true way, and walk in it, and you will find cleansing for your souls.
But they said, “We will not walk in it.”
I appointed watchmen among you: “Listen to the sound of the trumpet.”
But they said, “We will not listen.”’”
Therefore listen, you nations, and you who tend flocks among them.

And immediately afterward: Listen, earth! See, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their turning away, because they did not heed my words and rejected my law, which the prophets proclaimed.
I will show that the law is coming to an end not only by this alone, but also clearly by other proofs from the prophets.
The Jews answered him: Every Jew knows that this truly must happen, but does not know that the time of the Anointed One has come.

The philosopher said to them: Why do you put forward these objections, seeing that Jerusalem has been destroyed, the sacrifices have ceased, and everything the prophets foretold about you has happened?

For Malachi plainly cries out: I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept sacrifices from your hands, because from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place incense and a pure sacrifice are offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty.
They said: All these nations you speak of wish to be blessed and circumcised in the city of Jerusalem.

The philosopher said: Then how is it that Moses says: If you truly listen, keep the law in everything, and your borders will extend from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River Euphrates.

But we nations are blessed in that offspring of Abraham who came from the root of Jesse, who is called the hope of the nations and the light of all the earth and all the islands, and we are enlightened by the glory of God.
It is not according to that law or in that place that the prophets cry out so loudly.
For Zechariah said: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! See, your king comes to you, gentle, riding on a donkey’s colt, the offspring of a beast of burden.

And again: He will destroy the weapons of Ephraim and the horses of Jerusalem, and he will proclaim peace to the nations, and his dominion will extend from the edge of the earth to the ends of the inhabited world.
Jacob said: A prince will not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until the one comes for whom it is reserved, and he is the hope of the nations.
Seeing all these things accomplished and fulfilled, what other one are you waiting for?
For Daniel, taught by an angel, said: Seventy weeks until Christ the ruler—that is, four hundred and ninety years—to seal the vision of prophecy.
And what do you think is the iron kingdom that Daniel refers to in the statue?
They answered: The Roman kingdom.
The philosopher asked them: Who is the stone that was cut from the mountain without human hands?
They answered: The Anointed One.
Then they said again: If, then, we explain from the prophets and other evidence that he has already come, as you say, how does the Roman kingdom still hold power?
The philosopher answered: It does not hold power, for it has passed away like the others, according to the pattern of the statue; For our kingdom is not Roman, but Christ’s, as the prophet said:
“God will establish a heavenly kingdom that will never perish, and its rule will not be left to another people; it will crush and scatter all kingdoms, and it will stand forever.”
Is it not a Christian kingdom, now called by Christ’s name?
But the Romans devoted themselves to idols.
These rulers, however, one from this nation and tribe, another from that, reign in Christ’s name, as the prophet Isaiah also makes clear when he says to you:

“You have left your name as a surfeit for my chosen ones. The Lord will kill you, but he will give those who serve him a new name, which will be blessed throughout the earth; for they will bless the true God, and those who swear oaths on earth will swear by the God of heaven.”
Have not all the prophets’ predictions clearly spoken about Christ already been fulfilled?
For Isaiah describes his birth from a virgin, saying this: “Look, the virgin will conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they will name him Emmanuel,” which means “God with us.”

And Micah said: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel, and his origins are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.
Therefore he will give her up until the time when the woman giving birth [?] will give birth.”
And Jeremiah said: “Ask and see whether a male has given birth. For that day is great, unlike any other, and it will be a time of distress for Jacob, but he will be saved from it.”
And Isaiah said: “Before the woman in labor gave birth, before the birth came, she escaped pain and bore a male child.”
Again the Jews said: “We are the blessed offspring of Shem, blessed by our father Noah, but you are not.”
Explaining these things to them, he said: “Your father’s blessing is nothing other than praise of God; none of it extends to that man.
For it says this: ‘Blessed is the Lord, the God of Shem.’ But to Japheth, from whom we descend, he said: ‘May the Lord enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.’”
He continued explaining from the prophets and the other books, and did not leave them alone until they themselves said: “It is so, just as you say.”
Again they said: “How can you put your hope in a man and claim to be blessed, when the Scriptures curse such a person?”
The philosopher answered: “Then is David cursed or blessed?”
They said: “Greatly blessed.”
The philosopher said: “Then we too put our hope in the one in whom he put his hope.
For he said in the Psalms: ‘Even the man who was at peace with me, in whom I trusted.’”
But that man is Christ, who is also God.
And whoever puts his trust in a mere man, we too declare accursed.
Again they put forward another argument, saying: “How is it that you Christians reject circumcision, when Christ did not reject it but underwent it according to the law?”

The philosopher answered: “For the one who first said to Abraham, ‘Let this be a sign between you and me,’ himself came and fulfilled it. It had been observed from that time until his coming, but he did not allow it to continue beyond that; he gave us baptism.”
They said: “Then why did others before Abraham please God without receiving that sign, while Abraham received it?”

The philosopher answered: “None of those men is shown to have had two wives, but Abraham alone. For this reason God cuts that member of his, setting a boundary for him not to transgress any further, and gives Adam’s first union as an example for the others to follow.
He did the same to Jacob, injuring the sinew of his thigh because he had taken four wives.
When he understood the reason why this had been done, he was given the name Israel, that is, ‘the mind sees God,’ for after that he is not shown to have approached a woman.
But Abraham did not understand this.”
Again the Jews asked: “How can you claim to please God when you bow down to idols?”

The philosopher answered: “First learn to distinguish the terms: what an icon is and what an idol is. Then, with this understanding, do not attack Christians. For in your language there are ten terms for such a representation.

Now I ask you: was the tabernacle that Moses brought down from the mountain an image, or an image of an image? And did he skillfully make a corresponding image, with [?] and [?] and hair, and exquisite cherubim?
And since he made it in this way, [?] prayers, do you therefore honor and bow down to wood and skins and hair, rather than to God, who gave such an image at that time?
The same applies to Solomon’s temple, since it contained images of cherubim and angels and many other figures.
Likewise, we Christians make images of those who have pleased God and honor them, distinguishing what is good from demonic images.
For the Scriptures condemn those who sacrifice their sons and daughters.”
The Jews said: “How is it that you do not oppose God when you eat pork and hare?”
He answered them: “The first covenant commands, ‘Eat everything, just as you eat green plants.’ For all things are clean to the clean, but the conscience of the defiled has been defiled.
And at the creation God says, ‘Behold, everything is very good.’
But because of your gluttony he withheld a few of these things.
For it says, ‘Jacob ate and was satisfied, and the beloved one rebelled.’”
And again: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.
We have shortened this from a much longer account and set down these few things as a reminder.

Whoever wishes to seek these complete and holy discourses will find them in his books, as our teacher, Archbishop Methodius, set them out, dividing them into eight discourses; and there he will see the power of speech, which, through God’s grace, is like a burning flame against his opponents.
When the leading men heard his sweet and fitting words, they said to him:

“You have been sent here by God to build us up, and you have learned all the Scriptures from him. You have spoken of everything in order, satisfying us all to the full with the honey-sweet words of the Holy Scriptures.
But we are an unlettered people, and we believe this: that you are from God.
Above all, if you wish to bring peace to our souls, set everything right and explain to us in order, through parables, what we ask you.”
Then they dispersed to rest.
When they gathered the next day, they said to him: “Honorable man, explain to us through parables and reasoning which faith is the best of all.”
The philosopher answered them: “There was a married couple who were held in great honor by a certain king and were dearly loved.
But when they sinned, he drove them out and sent them away from his land.
They lived there for many years and had children in poverty.
Gathering their children around them, they took counsel about how they might return to their former position.
One of them advised one thing, another something else, and another something different again. Which advice, then, should they follow? Should it not be the best?”
They said: “Why do you speak in this way? Each person considers his own advice the best.
The Saracens do likewise, and others each have their own.
Tell us, then, which of these views is best.”
The philosopher said: “Fire tests gold and silver, and a person uses reason to distinguish falsehood from truth. [?] does so, then afterward it will bear sweet fruit.
Tell me: what caused the first fall? Was it not the sight of the sweet fruit and the desire to become divine?”
They said: “That is so.”
The philosopher said, “If someone becomes ill from eating honey or drinking cold water, and a physician comes and tells him, ‘Eat still more honey and recover,’
and tells the one who drank water, ‘Drink your fill of cold water and stand naked in the frost, and you will recover,’
but another physician does not speak this way, and instead prescribes the opposite treatment: ‘Fast, drinking something bitter instead of honey, and something warm and hot instead of cold water’—
which of the two treats people more skillfully?”
They all answered, “The one who prescribes opposites as treatment.”
“For the desire for pleasure must be put to death through the bitterness of this life, and pride through humility, treating opposites with opposites.
And we say that the tree which is at first a thorn [?]
For Christ’s law reveals the godly life through its sharpness, but afterward, in the eternal dwellings, it bears fruit a hundredfold.”
One of them, who knew the malice of the Saracens well, asked the philosopher, “Tell me, guest, why do you not follow Muhammad?

For he praised Christ greatly in his books, saying that he was born of a virgin, the sister of Moses, that he was a great prophet, and that he raised the dead and healed all kinds of sores by great power.”
The philosopher answered him, “Let the khagan judge [?].”
Then he said, “If Muhammad is a prophet, how can we believe Daniel?
For he said, ‘With Christ, every prophetic vision will cease.’
How, then, can this man be a prophet, having appeared after Christ?
For if we call him a prophet, we reject Daniel.”
Many of them said, “Daniel did indeed speak; he spoke by the Spirit of God.
But we all know that Muhammad is false and a destroyer of everyone’s salvation, who spewed out the finest of his ravings to promote wickedness and shameful deeds.”

Then their chief counselor said to the Saracen supporters: “With God’s help, this guest has cast all Jewish pride to the ground, and has thrown yours across to the other side of the river like something filthy.”

He also said to all the people, “Just as God has given the Christian emperor authority over all nations and perfect wisdom, so he has also placed faith among them, and apart from it no one can live an eternal life.
Glory to God forever.”
Then the philosopher said to everyone with tears, “Brothers, fathers, friends, and children, behold, God grants all understanding and a fitting answer.
If there is still anyone who opposes this, let him come and refute it, or be refuted.”
Whoever accepts this, let him be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity.
But if anyone is unwilling, I am free of this sin, and he will see on the Day of Judgment, when the Ancient of Days sits as God to judge all nations.
They answered, “We too are not enemies to ourselves.
But little by little, as each is able, we command that whoever wishes should be baptized willingly, from this day onward.
But anyone among you who bows toward the west, prays in the Jewish manner, or holds the Saracen faith will quickly receive death at our hands.”
And so they parted with joy.
About two hundred people among them were baptized, renouncing pagan abominations and unlawful marriages.
The khagan wrote a letter to the emperor as follows: “You have sent us, lord, such a man as has explained the Christian faith to us in words and deeds, showing it to be holy.
And having become convinced that this is the true faith, we have commanded that people be baptized of their own free will, hoping that we too may attain the same.
We are all friends of your empire and ready to serve you wherever you need us.”
As the khagan sent the Philosopher on his way, he offered him many gifts, but he did not accept them, saying: “Give me as many Greek prisoners as you have here; that is greater to me than all gifts.”
They gathered about two hundred of them and handed them over to him, and he went on his way rejoicing.
When they reached waterless, deserted places, they could not endure their thirst.
They found water in a salt marsh, but they could not drink it, for it was like gall.
When everyone had gone off to look for water, he said to his brother Methodius, “I cannot endure this thirst; draw some of this water.
For he who once changed bitter water into sweet for the Israelites will also bring us relief.”
They drew some and found it sweet as honey and cold.
And the two of them drank and glorified God, who does such things for his servants.
While dining with the archbishop in Cherson, the Philosopher said to him, “Pray for me, father, as my own father would have done.”
When some people privately asked him why he had done this, the Philosopher answered, “Truly, tomorrow he will depart from us to the Lord and leave us.”
And so it happened, and these words were fulfilled.

Among the people of Phullae there was a great oak that had grown together with a cherry tree, and beneath it they offered sacrifices, calling it Alexander and allowing no women to approach it or its sacrifices.

When the Philosopher heard this, he did not shrink from the trouble of traveling to them, and standing in their midst, he said to them: The Greeks have gone to eternal torment, having worshiped heaven and earth as God, and likewise the great and beautiful creation.
Then how will you, who worship wood, a worthless thing ready for the fire, escape eternal fire?
They answered, “We have not only now begun doing this, but have inherited it from our fathers, and from it we obtain everything we ask for: rain and many other things besides.”
“And how shall we do this, which none of us has dared to do?”
“For if anyone dares to do this, he will immediately meet death, and we shall never see rain again.”
The philosopher answered them, “God speaks about you in the Scriptures; how, then, can you reject him?”

For Isaiah cries out on the Lord’s behalf, saying: “I am coming to gather all tribes and all nations, and they will come and see my glory. I will set a sign among them and send survivors from among them to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Meshech, Tubal, Greece, and the distant islands, which have not heard my name, and they will proclaim my glory among the nations,” says the Lord Almighty.
And again: “Behold, I will send many fishermen and hunters, and they will catch you on the hills and among the rocky cliffs.”
“Brothers, acknowledge God, who created you. This is the gospel of God’s new covenant, into which you were baptized.”
Having persuaded them with gentle words in this way, he commanded them to cut down the tree and burn it.
Their elder bowed down, went forward, and kissed the Gospel book, and everyone else did likewise.
Having received white candles from the philosopher, they went to the tree singing. Taking an axe, he struck it thirty-three times and ordered everyone to cut it down, uproot it, and burn it.
That very night, rain immediately came from God.
They praised God with great joy, and God rejoiced greatly over this.
The philosopher went to Constantinople.
After seeing the emperor, he stayed in the Church of the Holy Apostles, praying to God.
In Hagia Sophia there is a chalice made of precious stone, the work of Solomon. On its sides are inscriptions in Hebrew and Samaritan letters, which no one could either read or explain.
The philosopher took it, read them, and explained them.
It reads as follows: “Prophesy, until [?] the star; be a drink for the Lord, the firstborn, who keeps watch at night.”
Then, on the second side: “Made from another tree for the Lord to taste: drink, become drunk with joy, and cry out, ‘Alleluia!’”
And then, on the third side: “Behold the prince, and the whole assembly will see his glory, and David will be in their midst.”
And after this the number nine hundred and nine is written.
The philosopher calculated carefully and found that there were nine hundred and nine years from the twelfth year of King Solomon to the birth of Christ.
This is a prophecy about Christ.
While the philosopher was rejoicing in God, another matter arose, bringing a task no less demanding than the earlier ones.
For Rastislav, prince of Moravia, prompted by God, took counsel with his Moravian princes and sent a message to Emperor Michael, saying:

“Our people have rejected paganism and follow the Christian faith, but we have no teacher who can explain the true Christian faith to us in our own language, so that other lands, seeing this, might follow our example.
So send us, lord, such a bishop and teacher.
For the good law goes out from you to every land.”
The emperor assembled a council, summoned Constantine the philosopher, had him hear this message, and said:
“I know that you are weary, philosopher, but you must go there.
For no one else can accomplish this task as you can.”
The philosopher answered, “Though I am weary and ill in body, I will gladly go there, if they have letters for their own language.”
The emperor said to him, “My grandfather, my father, and many others searched for these but did not find them. How, then, can I find them?”
The philosopher said, “Who can write words on water and earn himself the name of heretic?”
The emperor answered him again, together with Bardas and his own [?]: “If you wish, God can grant this to you, for he gives to everyone who asks without doubting and opens to those who knock.”
The philosopher went away and, following his former custom, devoted himself to prayer together with his other helpers.

God soon revealed the letters to him, hearing the prayers of his servants. He immediately formed the letters and began to write the words of the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and so on.
The emperor rejoiced and glorified God with his counselors. He sent him with many gifts, writing a letter to Rastislav as follows:

“God, who commands everyone to come to the knowledge of the truth and attain a higher standing, has seen your faith and striving and has now acted in our own time, revealing letters for your language—something that had not happened before, except in the earliest times—so that you too may be counted among the great nations that glorify God in their own language.
And we have also sent you the man to whom God revealed them, an honorable and devout man, a philosopher of great learning.
Accept this gift, greater and more precious than all gold, silver, precious stones, and perishable wealth.”

Act promptly together with him, and establish the word, seeking God with all your heart. Do not reject the salvation offered to all, but urge everyone not to be lazy, but to take the true path, so that you too, having brought them to the knowledge of God through your efforts, may receive your reward for this, both in this age and in the age to come, for all the souls who wish to believe in Christ our God from now until the end, leaving your memory to future generations, like the great Emperor Constantine.
When he arrived in Moravia, Rastislav received him with great honor, gathered pupils, and entrusted them to him to teach.
He soon took up the entire order of church worship and taught them Matins, the Hours, Vespers, Compline, and the sacred liturgy.
And, according to the prophetic word, the ears of the deaf were opened, and they heard the words of Scripture, and the tongues of those who stammered became clear.
God rejoiced at this, but the devil was put to shame.

As God's teaching spread, the evil, envious devil, thrice accursed from the beginning, could not bear this good, but entered his own vessels and began stirring up many people, saying to them, “God is not glorified by this.
For if this had been pleasing to him, could he not have arranged for these people too, from the beginning, to write their own language in letters and glorify God?
But he has chosen only three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—in which it is fitting to give glory to God.”
Those saying this were members of the Latin clergy: bishops, priests, and pupils.

He fought against them as David fought against the foreigners, defeated them with the words of Scripture, and called them trilingualists, because Pilate had written this way on the inscription over the Lord.

They not only said this, but also taught other impieties, saying that people with large heads live beneath the earth, that every creeping creature is the devil's creation, and that anyone who kills a snake will be freed from nine sins because of it; if anyone kills a person, he must drink from a wooden cup for three months and not touch a glass one.
And they did not forbid sacrifices according to the old custom, or dishonorable marriages.
He cut all this down like thorns and burned it with the fire of his words, saying: “Offer God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.
Do not dismiss the wife of your youth; for if you hate her and dismiss her, it will not cover the dishonor of your desire, says the Lord Almighty.

Guard yourselves in your spirit, so that none of you abandons the wife of his youth. Yet you have done these things that I hated, for he bore witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have abandoned; she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.”

And in the Gospel the Lord says: “You have heard that it was said by those of old, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman with desire for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
And again: “I tell you that whoever dismisses his wife, except on grounds of sexual immorality, causes her to commit adultery; and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery.”
The apostle said: “What God has joined together, let no one separate.”
He spent forty months in Moravia and then went to take his disciples away.
As he traveled, Kocel, prince of Pannonia, received him. Having grown very fond of Slavonic books, he learned to read them and entrusted him with up to eight disciples to learn them.
He showed him great honor and escorted him on his way.
He took neither gold nor silver nor anything else from either Rastislav or Kocel, taking the gospel saying as his rule, and without food.
He asked only for nine hundred captives from the two of them and set them free.
When he was in Venice, bishops, priests, and monks gathered against him like ravens against a falcon and raised the three-language heresy, saying:

“Tell us, man, how have you now created books for the Slavs and begun teaching them, when no one else devised them before—not an apostle, nor a pope of Rome, nor Gregory the Theologian, nor Jerome, nor Augustine?
We know only three languages in which it is fitting to glorify God in books: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.”
The Philosopher answered them: “Does not rain fall from God equally upon everyone? And does not the sun likewise shine upon everyone? Do we not all breathe the air equally?
How, then, are you not ashamed to recognize only three languages and command all other nations and tribes to be blind and deaf?
Tell me: do you make God powerless, as though he could not grant this, or envious, as though he did not wish to?
We know peoples who have books and give glory to God, each in their own language.
These are well known: Armenians, Persians, Abkhazians, Iberians, Sogdians, Goths, Avars, Turks, Khazars, Arabs, Egyptians, and many others.
But if you will not understand from these examples, at least recognize the Judge from the Scriptures.
For David cries out, saying: ‘Sing to the Lord, all the earth; sing a new song to the Lord.’
And again: ‘Shout to the Lord, all the earth; sing, rejoice, and sing praises.’
And elsewhere: ‘Let all the earth bow down to you and sing to you, and let it sing to your name, O Most High.’
And again: ‘Praise the Lord, all nations, and praise him, all peoples,’ and ‘Let everything that breathes praise the Lord.’
In the Gospel he says: ‘As many as he received, he gave them authority to become children of God.’
And again, the same one says: ‘I ask not only for these, but also for those who believe in me through the word, that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you.’

Matthew said: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.’ Look, I am with you every day until the end of the age. Amen.
And Mark, in turn: Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to all creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
These signs will follow those who believe: in my name they will drive out demons, and they will speak in new tongues.

He also says to you: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before people. For you do not enter yourselves, and you do not allow those who want to enter to do so.
And again: Woe to you, scribes, because you have taken away the key of understanding and have not entered yourselves.

Paul said to the Corinthians: I tell all of you to speak in tongues, but above all to prophesy. For the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the church too may be built up.
Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you, unless I speak to you through revelation and understanding, or through prophecy or teaching?
Even voiceless and lifeless things that give a sound, whether flutes or harps—if a distinction is made in their notes, how will the piping or harp-playing be recognized?
For if the trumpet gives a voiceless sound, who will prepare for battle?
So too with you: if you utter unintelligible words with your tongue, how will what is being said be understood?
For you will be speaking into the air.
There are, perhaps, so many kinds of sounds in the world, and not one of them is voiceless.
If I do not know the meaning of the sound, I will be a foreigner to the one speaking to me, and the speaker will be a foreigner to me.
So too with you: since you are eager for spiritual gifts, ask to abound in them for the building up of the church.
Therefore, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.
For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.
What then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, and I will also sing with the mind.
If you give a blessing with the spirit, how will someone in the position of an uninstructed person say Amen to your praise, since he does not know what you are saying?
You offer praise well enough, but the other person is not built up.
I praise my God; I speak in tongues more than you.
But in church I would rather speak five words with my mind, so that I may teach others too, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but mature in understanding.
It is written in the Law: “Through people of other languages and through other lips I will speak to these people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.”
Therefore tongues are a sign not for unbelievers but for believers, while prophecy is for unbelievers.
So if the whole church gathers together and everyone speaks in tongues, and someone unlearned or unbelieving comes in, will they not say that you are behaving badly?
But if everyone prophesies and someone unlearned or unbelieving comes in, he is convicted by everyone and examined by everyone.
And so the secrets of his heart become known; and so, falling facedown, he will worship God and declare that God is truly among you.
What then, brothers? When you gather, each of you has a psalm—let him keep it—and has a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let everything be done to build people up.
If anyone speaks in a tongue, let two or three speak, taking turns, and let one interpret.
But if there is no interpreter, let him remain silent in church and speak to himself and to God.
Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others interpret.
But if something is revealed to another who has knowledge, let the first remain silent.
For you can all prophesy one at a time, so that everyone may be encouraged.
And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.
God is not a God of disorder but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints.
Let your women remain silent in the churches, for they are not permitted to speak, but must be submissive, as the Law also says.
If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands in their own homes, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
Or did the word of God come from you? Or was it found among you alone?
And if anyone thinks he is a prophet or a spiritual person, let him recognize that what I write to you is the Lord’s commandments.
But if anyone does not understand, let him understand.
Therefore, brothers, understand prophecy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.
Let everything be done properly and in order.
And again he says: “And every tongue will confess him, that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God and the Father. Amen.”
Having put them to shame with these words and other, greater ones, he departed, leaving them.
And when the pope of Rome learned about him, he sent for him.
And when he arrived in Rome, the apostolic pope Adrian [?] came out with all the citizens, carrying candles, because he was also bringing the relics of Saint Clement, the martyr and pope of Rome.
And immediately God began to work miracles.
A paralyzed man was healed there, and many others were freed from various illnesses. Even captives, after calling upon Christ and Saint Clement, escaped from [?].
The pope received the Slavonic books, blessed them, and placed them in the Church of Saint Mary, which is called Photida, and they celebrated the liturgy over them.
After this, the pope ordered two bishops, Formosus and Gauderic, to ordain the Slavonic disciples with spoken words.
And when they had been ordained, they immediately celebrated the liturgy in the Slavonic language in the Church of the Holy Apostle Peter.
And on the next day they celebrated it in the Church of Saint Petronilla.

And on the following day, in the Church of Saint Andrew, and from there again in the church of the great teacher of the whole world, Paul the Apostle. And all night they sang in Slavonic and celebrated the liturgy over the holy tomb, with the help of Arsenius, a bishop who was one of the seven bishops, and Anastasius the librarian.
And the Philosopher, together with his disciples, never ceased to give God fitting praise for this.
The Romans kept coming to him and questioning him, and they received explanations from him twofold and threefold.

A certain Jew also used to come and debate with him, and once said to him: “According to the reckoning of the years, Christ has not yet come—the one of whom the prophets say that he is to be born of a virgin.”

The Philosopher counted out for him all the years from Adam, generation by generation, and explained to him in detail that Christ had come and how many years had passed from then until the present. And after instructing him, he sent him away.
And many hardships overtook him, and he fell ill.

As he endured [?] for many days, he once saw a divine apparition and began to sing as follows: “My spirit rejoiced and my heart was glad because of those who said to me, ‘Let us enter the house of the Lord.’”

And he put on honorable robes and remained that way throughout the day, rejoicing and saying: “From now on I am no longer a servant of the emperor or of anyone else on earth, but only of God Almighty.
I was not, and I came to be, and I am forever. Amen.”
On the following day he put on the holy monastic habit, and, receiving light upon light, took the name Cyril.
And he remained in that habit for eight days.
And as the hour drew near for him to be received back and depart to the eternal dwellings, he raised his hands to God and prayed with tears, saying:

“O Lord my God, you who established all the ranks of angels and the bodiless powers, stretched out heaven and founded the earth, and brought everything that exists from nonexistence into being; you who always and everywhere listen to those who do your will, fear you, and keep your commandments: hear my prayer and preserve your faithful flock, over which you placed your useless and unworthy servant.

Deliver them from the godless and pagan malice of those who speak blasphemy against you, destroy the trilingual heresy, increase your Church in numbers, and bring everyone together in unity and make them a chosen people, united in your true faith and right confession, and breathe into their hearts the word of adoption as your children.
For it is your gift that you have accepted us, unworthy as we are, to proclaim the gospel of your Christ, urging ourselves toward good deeds and doing what pleases you.

What you had given me, I hand over to you as your own. Uphold them with your mighty right hand; shelter them beneath the covering of your wings, so that everyone may praise and glorify your name, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Then he greeted everyone with a holy kiss and said: “Blessed is God, who has not given us as prey to the teeth of our invisible enemies, but has broken their snare and delivered us from their destruction.”
And so he rested in the Lord at the age of forty-two, in the month of February, on the fourteenth day, in the second indiction, in the year 6370 from the creation of the whole world.

And the pope ordered all the Greeks who were in Rome, and likewise the Romans, who had gathered with candles, to sing over him and give him a funeral procession such as they would have given the pope himself.
And this they did.

Methodius, his brother, made a request of the pope, saying: “Our mother bound us by an oath that whichever of us went first to judgment, the other should bring him to the monastery of his brethren and bury him there.”
The pope ordered him to be placed in a coffin and fastened shut with iron nails. They kept him like this for seven days, preparing for the journey.
But the Roman bishops said to the pope: “Since God brought him here after he had traveled through many lands, and took his soul here, it is fitting that he should lie here as an honorable man.”
And the pope said: “Because of his holiness and love, [?] Roman custom, I will bury him in my own tomb in the Church of the Holy Apostle Peter.”
But his brother said: “Since you have not listened to me and will not give him to me, if it pleases you, let him lie in the Church of Saint Clement, with whom he came here.”
And the pope ordered this to be done.
The bishops gathered again with all the people, wishing to escort him with honor, and the bishops said: “Let us remove the nails from the coffin and see whether anything has been taken from him.”
They labored hard, but by God's command they could not remove the nails from the coffin.
So they placed him, together with the coffin, in a tomb on the right side of the altar in the Church of Saint Clement, where many miracles immediately began to take place.
Because of these, the Romans [?] became still more devoted to his holiness and honor.
They painted an image of him above his tomb and began to keep lights burning over him day and night, praising God, who thus glorifies those who glorify him.
For to him belong glory and honor throughout all ages. Amen.
